questions.question: Given a basis matrix B with columns b1,…,bn in R^m, what is the lattice L(B)?
options: All real linear combinations of the basis vectors: {B x : x ∈ R^n}
All integer linear combinations of the basis vectors: {B z : z ∈ Z^n}
All vectors whose Euclidean norm is at most max(||b1||,…,||bn||)
All points inside the fundamental parallelepiped {B x : x ∈ [0,1)^n}
questions.explanation: A lattice is the integer span of a basis: every point is Bz for some integer vector z.

questions.question: What makes a 2×2 integer matrix U unimodular?
options: U has entries in {−1,0,1} only
det(U) = ±1, so U maps Z^2 to Z^2 bijectively
U is orthogonal, so UᵀU = I
U has determinant 0, so it collapses one dimension
questions.explanation: Unimodular means integer matrix with determinant ±1; its inverse is also integer.

questions.question: Let b1 = (2,0), b2 = (1,1). What lattice point do you get from coefficients (z1,z2) = (3,−2)?
If U is unimodular, which statement is correct about the bases B and B' = B·U (column basis convention)?
options: They generate different lattices because the basis vectors changed
They generate the same lattice: L(B') = L(B)
They generate the same lattice only when det(U) = +1 (not −1)
They generate the same lattice only if U is orthogonal
questions.explanation: Unimodular U maps Z^n bijectively to Z^n, so {B(Uz)} = {Bz} as sets.

questions.question: In full rank R^n, what is the volume of the fundamental parallelepiped P(B) = {B x : x ∈ [0,1)^n}?
options: det(B), which can be negative and indicates orientation
|det(B)|, which is the lattice determinant det(L)
trace(B), since it adds up the basis directions
||b1||·…·||bn||, the product of basis vector lengths
questions.explanation: The cell volume is |det(B)|. Orientation can flip the sign, so volume uses absolute value.

questions.question: Suppose U is unimodular. Which identity always holds for determinants (square full-rank case)?
options: det(BU) = det(B)·det(U), so |det(BU)| = |det(B)|
det(BU) = det(B) + det(U), so |det(BU)| can grow
det(BU) = det(B)/det(U), so |det(BU)| is smaller for large |det(U)|
det(BU) = det(U) only, since U dominates the basis
questions.explanation: det(BU) = det(B)det(U). For unimodular U, det(U)=±1, so the absolute determinant is unchanged.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a lattice invariant (i.e., can change when you change the basis of the same lattice)?
options: The set of lattice points L(B)
The absolute determinant det(L) = |det(B)| (full rank)
The length of the first basis vector ||b1||
The set of norms of all lattice vectors {||v|| : v ∈ L(B)}
questions.explanation: A lattice can have many very different bases; individual basis-vector lengths are not intrinsic to the point set.

questions.question: Attack the wrong mental model: why is “publishing a basis with long vectors makes the lattice sparse and secure” false?
options: Because you can apply a unimodular change of basis that makes basis vectors longer or shorter without changing the lattice point set
Because a lattice always contains all real linear combinations of its basis, so density is unchanged
Because determinant is always 1 for integer bases, so all lattices have the same density
Because any long-vector basis must be orthogonal, which makes SVP easy
questions.explanation: Unimodular basis changes preserve the lattice. Making a basis “look long” does not remove short lattice vectors or change determinant.
